top_choice_rationale: Optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) are a new principle for neutral atoms, the magic-wavelength lattice that allows parallel interrogation of many atoms, reproduced independently at about 1e-18 by several laboratories with agreeing cross-comparisons. The prize has the cleanest two-name credit on the slate and a citation scoped to the invention and development of the clock; it has already enabled measurements such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and bounds on constants and ultralight dark matter. Topological insulators are a strong second, and I rank the Kane-Molenkamp-Hasan allocation above Kane-Mele-Molenkamp because it credits both experimental confirmations (HgTe transport and ARPES on bismuth-based crystals), though the third seat and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit remain unresolved. No award is last.
recusal_note: No direct tie to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile, but as a Lund atomic-physics laser spectroscopist I spent a year in John Hall's lab in Boulder, where Jun Ye later worked, and I share a loose WACQT/Chalmers link with Johansson (relevant to circuit QED, not to this slate); a possible recusal question on P002 should be noted but I complete the ballot.
